passages.subject: cartography / map projections
passages.text: Every flat map of a round world is wrong, and the only question is where the wrongness has been put. A projection that keeps areas true will distort shapes; one that keeps shapes true will distort areas; no projection keeps both, and this is not a limitation of present technique but a proof about surfaces. The Mercator projection, criticised for four centuries for making the high latitudes enormous, keeps something else instead: a straight line drawn on it is a line of constant compass bearing. For a navigator with a compass and a ruler that was not a convenience but the whole of the point, and it is the reason the projection was made at all. The criticism is therefore accurate and beside the point when it is aimed at the map, and well aimed when it is directed at the use. A projection built for steering a ship became, by habit and by printing, the map on every classroom wall, where nobody was steering anything and the only message it carried was relative size. Replacing it there was obviously right. What is less obvious, and tends to get lost in the argument, is that its replacements are wrong in their own ways and were chosen because their wrongness sits somewhere a classroom cares less about. There is no map that simply tells the truth. There are maps whose errors have been arranged to suit a particular question, and the honest ones are labelled with the question they were arranged for.

passages.subject: labour economics / the tip
passages.text: A tip is a payment made after the service has been given, by somebody under no obligation to make it, for a benefit he has already received. Every account of it in economics has to begin by explaining why it happens at all, and the explanations do not travel: the practice is close to compulsory in some countries, insulting in others, and in a third group it has been absorbed into the price and has disappeared. Where it survives it usually does two things that are worth separating. The first is to transfer part of the employer's wage bill to the customer, which is why the countries with the largest tips tend to be those with the lowest legal minimum for the staff who receive them. The second is to give the customer a small piece of authority over somebody whose income depends on his approval, and this is the part that defenders of the custom rarely mention and its critics rarely get right. The authority is real, but it is exercised almost at random: studies of the amounts actually left find them better predicted by the weather, the size of the party and the position of the table than by anything the server did. A system that claims to reward good service turns out to reward being served in a certain kind of room on a certain kind of day, which is a defensible way of distributing income only if nobody says out loud what it is doing.

passages.subject: criminal law / the public prosecutor
passages.text: For most of English legal history there was no public prosecutor. A crime was prosecuted by the person it had been committed against, who paid for it, employed the lawyer and could drop the case at any point and for any reason, including a payment from the accused. The system had two consequences that followed from it directly. Wealthy victims got prosecutions and poor ones did not, and a great many offences were settled privately in a manner that is now called blackmail and was then called a reasonable arrangement. The state took the job over slowly, and for reasons that had little to do with fairness to defendants: what the state wanted was a decision about whether to prosecute that was not for sale. The change brought a difficulty nobody had faced before. A private prosecutor acts for himself, and nobody expects anything else of him. A public one acts for an abstraction, and the question of what the abstraction wants has no obvious answer. The victim may want a trial, the police may want a conviction, the public purse wants neither if the case is weak, and the accused has an interest that is not represented at all until the trial begins. Modern codes meet this with a two-part test about evidence and public interest, which sounds procedural and is in fact the whole of the problem written down. The prosecutor who applies it is deciding, case by case, what the abstraction wants.

passages.subject: early history / grain and the state
passages.text: Of all the plants that early farmers grew, the ones that became the foundation of states were the cereals, and the reason is not that they are the most nourishing. Roots and tubers yield more food per unit of land in many climates, and they keep perfectly well where they are. That last property is the difficulty. A crop that can be left in the soil and dug up as it is wanted cannot easily be counted, cannot be seized on a particular day, and cannot be stored in one place by anybody other than the farmer. Grain is the opposite in every respect. It ripens at a known time, it has to be harvested within a short window, it is visible above ground while it grows, and once harvested it is dense, durable and divisible. Every one of these is a convenience for the grower and an opportunity for a tax collector, and the second is what mattered historically. A state is in the first instance a thing that takes a share and keeps records, and both operations need a crop that arrives on a schedule and then sits in a heap. Archaeologists working on the earliest state formations have found granaries and tallies before they have found palaces, which is the order the argument predicts. The cereal did not feed the state because it was better food. It fed the state because it could be counted.

passages.subject: environmental law / noise
passages.text: Noise was the last of the common nuisances to become something the law could grip. Smoke could be seen, waste could be weighed, and a structure that overhung a neighbour's land could be described by a surveyor; a sound stops the moment anybody arrives to examine it and leaves nothing behind. For centuries the response was to treat it as a matter between neighbours, which worked while the loudest thing in a street was a cart. Industrial machinery and then amplified music made the problem large enough to need a rule, and the rule had to wait for an instrument. The decibel scale gave courts something they could put into a judgment, and for a while it appeared to have settled the matter. It had not, because the quantity that can be measured and the quantity that does the harm are not the same. A sound that is steady is easier to live beside than one that stops and starts at the same level; a sound with a meaning in it, such as a voice or a repeated bass note, is harder again; and a sound a person believes to be unnecessary is harder than an identical sound he believes nobody could have helped. None of this appears on the meter. Modern regulations therefore mix a measured limit with a test about what a reasonable person would tolerate, which is an admission that the number by itself decides too little.
